summary: Reports the results of a survey of BGP-4 implementations with 259 questions about support for the protocol specified in RFC 4271. It gives a brief summary and then lists each response. Four implementers completed the survey and three gave brief information. The editors did not independently verify the answers.

plainLanguage.summary: A long quiz given to router makers about their products, with the answers written down. Nobody checked whether the answers were true.

questions: how well do bgp implementations match the spec
subtitle: A survey of how router vendors implement the core BGP-4 routing protocol.

tldr.problem: BGP-4 was a new Internet standard, and it was unclear whether vendors implemented it consistently or if their products could interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: A survey asked four major router vendors (Alcatel, Cisco, Laurel, NextHop) 259 detailed questions about their BGP-4 implementations, covering everything from message formats to error handling to the finite state machine.
tldr.outcome: Most vendors answered the same way, but significant differences emerged on 8 key requirements, revealing incompatibilities that would affect real deployments.

today: RFC 4276 is Informational. It remains part of the historical record of how BGP-4 was standardized and shows that despite minor implementation differences, the four major vendors could interoperate.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC reports the results of a survey designed to check how well vendors followed the BGP-4 specification (RFC 4271). As BGP-4 was being elevated from Draft Standard to Internet Standard, it was important to know whether implementations actually matched the spec and could work together.

The survey contained 259 detailed questions about implementation support for the features and behaviors specified in RFC 4271. Four companies completed the survey (Alcatel, Cisco, Laurel, and NextHop), and three others (Avici, Data Connection Ltd., and Nokia) provided brief information by phone. The editors did not verify the answers independently; they relied on the vendors' own expertise.
sections.plainLanguage: Before saying a rulebook is ready for the big leagues, people asked the main rule-followers: Do you do all of this? Four said yes or no to 259 questions each.

sections.title: Survey Results and Key Differences
sections.content:
The survey asked vendors to answer Y (yes), N (no), or O (other/alternate behavior) for each question, based on RFC 2119 keywords like MUST, SHOULD, and MAY. Most questions received consistent affirmative responses from at least two vendors, but some critical requirements showed disagreement.

The most significant differences appeared in requirements marked MUST (meaning implementations are required to do them): nine MUST questions had split answers, including requirements about linked route aggregation logic. For SHOULD questions (recommended behaviors), 25 showed disagreement, and MAY questions (optional behaviors) showed variation as expected.

A linked pair of questions about route aggregation stood out: three vendors answered N to whether they aggregate routes when both routes have the same NEXT_HOP attribute, even though their earlier answer suggested they understood the basic decision logic.
sections.plainLanguage: When asked whether they did every single thing required, almost all the companies said yes to most questions. But on eight really important rules (the MUST ones), at least one company said no, meaning it did something different.

sections.title: Interoperability Findings
sections.content:
The survey included an interoperability matrix showing which implementations had been tested together. All four major vendors reported successful interoperability with at least one other vendor, and Cisco had been verified to work with three of the others. Alcatel was paired with Cisco and Laurel with Cisco and NextHop.

This testing showed that despite differences in their answers, vendors could still exchange routing information. However, the differences revealed in this survey explain why operators sometimes find that policies or behaviors work differently on different vendor platforms.
sections.plainLanguage: The four companies had actually tested whether their routers could talk to each other. They could, even where their answers differed slightly.

sections.title: Coverage of BGP-4 Requirements
sections.content:
The survey was comprehensive, covering all the major sections of RFC 4271: routes and storage, routing information bases, message formats (OPEN, UPDATE, KEEPALIVE, NOTIFICATION), path attributes (ORIGIN, AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, MULTI_EXIT_DISC, LOCAL_PREF, ATOMIC_AGGREGATE, AGGREGATOR), error handling, finite state machine, update handling, route selection, and timers.

For each requirement, the survey noted which RFC 2119 keyword applied (MUST, SHALL, SHOULD, MAY, etc.), making it easy to see which answers showed deviation from mandatory behavior versus optional behavior. An optional disagreement was less concerning than disagreement on a MUST requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: The questions covered every part of the BGP rulebook: how to store routes, how to format messages, how to pick the best route, how to handle errors, and when to send messages.

sections.title: Why This Survey Mattered
sections.content:
RFC 4271 was already widely deployed in the Internet; BGP had been running since 1989 and BGP-4 since 1993. However, standardization rules required demonstrating that a protocol was well understood and stable before advancing it to a higher maturity level. This survey provided evidence that implementers understood the spec, that they had built working systems, and that those systems could interoperate.

The survey also revealed where implementations diverged, helping the IETF understand which parts of the spec might need clarification in the future and where operators needed to be aware of vendor differences.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP was already working in the real world, but the rulebook wanted proof that everyone understood the game the same way. This survey gave that proof, even though a few teams played a corner of the game slightly differently.

references.text: Rekhter, Y., Li, T., and S. Hares, Eds., "A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4)", RFC 4271, January 2006.
